notes: Brightwater's roads round the Mere: the Fair Company's writ-sellers on the south shore, the Hush-sellers' runners by night, the Tallymen's clerks and the laundresses by day, the eel-carts out of Gullhithe and the slate wagons off the east shore (docs/WORLD_LIFE_ROADS.md).

lines.speaker: A bravo
lines.spring: The toll on this road is everything you're carrying.

name: The Fair Company's writ-sellers
notes: Pennyfold's bravos selling protection on the south shore (pois/brightwater.json pennyfold_keep). Not once their captain is dealt with.

folk.name: A carter with a torn writ

talk.say: They said nine wasn't eleven. -- Behind you!

lines.speaker: A Company blade
lines.spring: Writ of protection, friend? No? Then by the Charter you're not protected, and I'm obliged to show you what that means.

name: Hush-sellers' runners
notes: The Word-Seller's people moving stock from the Hush Hole to the Undercroft by night; a Hushed sayer keeps them quiet, so the tell is the crows or a tree across the road.

lines.speaker: A Hushed runner
lines.spring: Didn't hear us coming? Nobody does. That's what he charges for.

name: A Tallymen's clerk on his rounds

talk.say: Counting. Carts, sacks, feet, whatever the charter asks for this week. -- You've come past something on the road that isn't on my list. Off that way, at {place}. If you find anything there with a price on it, the Row will want to know first.

hook.rumour: The Tallymen's clerk has {place} down as not yet assessed.

consequence.notice: The Tallymen will have that in a ledger by morning.

talk.say: Over the Stride twice a week for the soft water at the Wash-Stones, basket on the hip, and the Fair Company wave us through without a penny, which is the only kind thing they do. -- There's a shirt came up in the wash last week none of us brought. A Sayer's, with a name in the collar. Nobody can read the name. Everybody's tried.

hook.rumour: The laundresses beat Tollmere's washing at {place}, where the water is soft.

talk.say: I copied the Ledger of Prices for a year and I got to the line with my own village in it. I'm not going back. -- There's a place off the road where nobody's counted anything. Go and look, if you want. Take this. It's the only thing I have that hasn't got a price in the Ledger.

hook.rumour: The apprentice says nobody has ever counted anything at {place}.

talk.prompt: Point the hunters after the apprentice
talk.say: The Row pays by the head, and he's a head. Here's your share, and it's a fair one.

name: An eel-cart out of Gullhithe
notes: Gullhithe's smoked eel going round the west shore to Sedgehithe, a packhorse and one guard.

talk.say: Smoked this morning, split side to the Lamp. Forty marks a barrel on the Row, and a good deal less off the back of my horse, because the Row isn't here.
Watch the fen side after the Eelweir. Leech-hounds come up the channel at night and they like eel as much as anybody.

consequence.notice: Gullhithe will hear an eel-cart was set on, and so will the Tallymen who tax it.
consequence.killing_notice: An eel-cart's guard lies dead on the shore road.

rescue.say: They'd have had the lot, horse and all. Here -- a barrel's worth, and a cut of the best, and you'll never pay Row prices at Gullhithe again.

name: A Cadbrae slate wagon
notes: The Slades' blue slate going round the south shore from the east landing to the Stride's Foot for the city; a heavy wagon and two guards.

talk.say: Cadbrae blue for the Row's new roof, a thousand to the load. Not the singing ones; Barnet won't send those. -- I've a few other bits on the tail if you're buying.
Slate doesn't look worth stealing till you know what a roof costs in Tollmere. Keep walking, friend.

consequence.notice: The Tallymen will want to know why a charter load was stopped.
consequence.killing_notice: A slate carter's man is dead on the road, and the Tallymen keep count.

rescue.say: There's a roof in Tollmere owes you, and it doesn't know it. Here, from the Slades' purse; Barnet would want it.

name: A split salt-sack and a tithe-clerk

talk.prompt: Help the carter sweep up the salt
talk.say: Quick, quick, before she's got her scale out -- every grain back in the sack and it's a sack, not a spill, and a sack's paid for. -- There. Take a twist for your trouble. You never saw the seal.

talk.prompt: Help the clerk weigh what spilled
talk.say: Thank you. Hold the pan. -- Four stone. Four stone, in an unsealed sack, on a cart from the west shore. That is the Weighmaster's sum exactly; Prudence Gauge at the Charter Scale will want to hear it from somebody who isn't me.

hook.rumour: A tithe-clerk weighed four stone of unsealed salt on the shore road and sent word to {place}.

name: Mourners carrying a boat to the water

talk.prompt: Walk a while with the mourners
talk.say: We're taking old Ansel down to the water. A Lakefolk goes out in his own boat with a lamp in her bow and lets the Mere have them both. Ansel had no boat, so the widows at the Keels lent him the Kettle, God love them, and chalked her off their board for it. -- Walk with us if you like. It's the custom to say his name once at the water.

hook.rumour: The widows at {place} lend a boat to anyone who goes out to the Mere without one.

talk.prompt: Help him pick up the shells
talk.say: The strap went and they're everywhere and if I lose one with a pearl in it Dilly'll skin me. -- That one, by your foot, and that -- there. Every one. Here, open that one yourself, it's yours, she won't know.

name: A silent salt-train in the dark

talk.say: *(He says nothing at all. He lays a finger on his lips, knocks once on the pack-saddle, and turns back the sailcloth.)*
*(He puts a white finger on your lips, hard. Then he points south-east along the shore, and knocks twice on his own chest: the fair. Tonight. Say nothing.)*

hook.rumour: Hooded salt-runners walk the shore roads by night to the fair at {place}, and say nothing.

name: A salvor with a sack of bronze

talk.say: Bronze from the Quarter, for the Row, and I'm not to stop till it's weighed. -- You'll have heard. The Patience came up empty three weeks back and the chain rings on its own every hour, and the Company won't send anybody down after the master. His girl sits at the windlass on the west tail and turns it a quarter every hour. Somebody ought to go down. Not me. I've a sack to carry.

hook.rumour: The Fathom Company's bell came up empty at {place}, and its chain rings by itself every hour.
